items.title: Most Roman emperors died violently
items.claim: Of the 69 Roman emperors from Augustus (27 BCE) to Theodosius I (395 CE), how many died of natural causes?

options.text: Almost all — emperors were generally well-protected
Roughly a third — the rest died by assassination, in battle, by suicide or under suspicious circumstances
All emperors after Nero were murdered

items.reveal:
Joseph Saleh and colleagues (2019) modelled imperial deaths and found violent end rates above 50% for the first 25 years of any reign. The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284) saw around 50 emperors and usurpers in 50 years.

Named assassinations: Caligula (41), Claudius (54, probably poisoned by Agrippina), Domitian (96), Commodus (192), Caracalla (217), Elagabalus (222) and many more. Some died in war (Decius at Abrittus, 251; Valerian captured by the Persians, 260).
items.why: The imperial succession looks orderly from the list of names. Statistically, becoming emperor was one of the most dangerous jobs in the ancient world — which itself shaped imperial policy.

items.title: British abolition came in two acts, decades apart

options.text: 1807 — both the trade and slavery itself

The Slave Trade Act 1807 abolished the trade; the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 ended slavery in most British colonies from August 1834 — with £20 million paid in compensation to slave-owners, not the enslaved

items.reveal:
The 1833 Act freed around 800,000 people in the Caribbean, Mauritius and the Cape from 1 August 1834. Field workers became 'apprentices' for six years (ended in 1838 after protests). Around 46,000 claims paid out £20 million — roughly 40% of the Treasury's annual budget.

The loan to finance the compensation (UCL's 'Legacies of British Slave-ownership' project) was only paid off by the UK Treasury in 2015. Slavery in British India was not covered by the 1833 Act; the Indian Slavery Act 1843 followed.

Wilberforce died on 29 July 1833, three days after the Act passed the Commons.
items.why: Abolition is celebrated as moral progress. The financial mechanics — owners compensated, the enslaved given six more years of forced labour, taxpayers paying off the loan until 2015 — complicate the story without erasing it.

items.title: Magna Carta was annulled within ten weeks
items.claim: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. What happened next?

options.text: It immediately became the basis of English liberty and was respected by the crown
John wrote to Pope Innocent III, who annulled it as 'shameful and demeaning' on 24 August 1215 — civil war resumed
John was forced to confirm it in Parliament the following year
It was burned by the barons after John refused to enforce it

items.reveal:
Pope Innocent III's bull of 24 August 1215 declared Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever', calling it extorted by force. The First Barons' War followed; the barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne.

John died of dysentery in October 1216. The charter was reissued by the regents of his nine-year-old son Henry III to win support — that is the version that took root. The 1297 reissue under Edward I is the one on the statute roll.
items.why: Magna Carta as 'the foundation of liberty' is a 17th-century invention (Coke). In 1215 it was a peace treaty between a desperate king and rebellious barons — and it failed within weeks.
